title: Dr. Martens Resoles: What Has to Come Off? | Brand Stories
description:
A customer in a public review first chose a repair and colours, then packed four-year-old boots in a shoebox. After the arrival notification, a separate authorised repair demonstration and the manufacturer's current explanations show how sole removal, welt stitching, heat welding and finishing move the work forward. We then return to that reviewer's account of completion, delivery and an extra set of laces. Public reviews remain attributed accounts that have not been independently verified. The images are anonymous conceptual illustrations; the demonstration and reviews do not establish that these are the same physical boots. The process temperature describes only the manufacturer's current sole-joining operation.

c7r20101.text: You've worn these boots for four years. The soles are almost worn through, but the uppers are still good. Which half would you want to keep?

c7r20102.text: In July 2025, someone sending their Dr. Martens for repair described this dilemma in a public review.

c7r20107.text: When choosing the repair, they could even pick the sole and stitching colours, which they found fun.

c7r20104.text: I want to follow along and see: how far does the repair have to take them apart?

c7h04b1.text: And what extra thing will be there when the parcel comes back?

c7r20105.text: Let's see whether this pair of Dr. Martens can keep the uppers their owner has worn in.

c7r20106.text: To keep those familiar uppers, what exactly has to be replaced?

c7r20203.text: One option mentions a welt. But where is it on the boot?

c7r20204.text: Look down from the upper: a strip runs around the edge of the boot, with stitching visible on it.

c7r20205.text: The repair service says welted footwear has a small visible gap at this point.

c7r20206.text: Viewed straight down, the sole also sticks out in a wider rim, rather than sitting flush with the upper.

c7r20207.text: Is that ring of stitching just decoration that makes the boot recognisable?

c7r20208.text: I used to see it as decoration. Up close, I notice it stitches an actual component in place.

c7r20209.text: That strip is called the welt, stitched to the lower edge of the upper. The website lists replacing the sole and welt as one repair.

c7r20234.text: What does the page currently charge to send a pair in for this repair?

c7r20210.text: The website currently lists a classic resole and new welt at £79.99 per pair.

c7r20213.text: That reviewer, meanwhile, felt their own repair cost less than buying another second-hand pair.

c7r20217.text: The upper is still good, but fold back the boot opening: if the heel lining has worn through, must the outer leather go too?

c7r20218.text: If the heel lining is worn through, the repair service can patch it or replace that lining with new leather.

c7r20219.text: They say repairing the heel lining can restore comfort and reduce further wear on the upper.

c7r20103.text: On Thursday, the reviewer put the boots in an old shoebox and printed the postage label. The next day, the postman collected it.

c7r20230.text: Once the boots are sent off, what news will the wearer receive first?

c7r20231.text: This customer says that when the repair service received the boots, it first sent a notification that they had arrived.

c7r20233.text: What will the repairer's knife remove from the boot first?

c7r20301.text: The authorised resole page says the old outsole, welt and stitching are removed first. In the demonstration, the repairer holds a boot upside down and runs a knife along the top edge of the sole.

c7r20302.text: You can still see the old stitching around the edge. The blade moves nearby, and the old join starts to separate.

c7r20303.text: Next, the inner layers underneath the boot are exposed. The whole outer sole that used to touch the ground is gone.

c7r20305.text: I'd watch the exposed joining area: which tool will the repairer take it to next?

c7r20307.text: The camera then points at the upturned bottom. A nozzle approaches the exposed layer, while the repairer wraps the hand holding the boot in cloth.

c7r20308.text: Sole up and shaft down, the repairer holds the whole upper together, without taking the leather apart into separate pieces.

c7r20310.text: Will the new outsole be stitched straight onto the upper?

c7r20313.text: In the demonstration, the boot turns around the machine needle as the new welt is attached first. According to the manufacturer's method, that strip is made of polyvinyl chloride.

c7r20314.text: As the machine stitches forward, the repairer's hands adjust, guiding the three-dimensional boot past the needle.

c7r20319.text: With the welt sewn on, the repairer turns the bottom towards a finishing tool and rotates the boot to work around the edge.

c7r20320.text: The pale underlayer faces out, and the black edge approaches the machine. This rim is worked on before the new outsole is attached.

c7r20322.text: How will it be joined so this boot, with its inner layers still exposed, can walk again?

c7r20401.text: Now comes heat welding. The repairer takes the new outsole and positions it underneath the upper with its welt already stitched on.

c7r20402.text: The company says most of today's outsoles use a polyvinyl chloride alloy: the plastic commonly called PVC.

c7r20403.text: Granules are melted and moulded into a sole, giving it a forefoot, a heel and the shape beneath your foot.

c7r20404.text: For the familiar air cushioning, the manufacturer describes air pockets in the soles of its Originals range as providing comfort and shock absorption.

c7r20405.text: The repairer adjusts the positions of the sole and upper, ready to join this new part to the rim just stitched on.

c7r20406.text: I thought the stitching would be enough, but now a hot blade appears. How hot is this sole-joining operation?

c7r20407.text: For this sole-joining operation, the manufacturer specifies a heat-welding temperature above 650 degrees.

c7r20408.text: The hot blade heats the joint, then rollers press the welt and outsole together.

c7r20409.text: As the tool touches the boot's edge, how are the other sections of the rim fed past it?

c7r20410.text: In the footage, an orange-red glow shows at the edge as the joining tool approaches. Both hands still support the sides of the boot.

c7r20411.text: The repairer turns the boot in another direction, bringing the section that faced them back towards the machine.

c7r20412.text: From the side, you can see the new sole's top edge meet the welt. The two parts that were separate now come together around the rim.

c7r20413.text: Once the heat-welding tool is removed, what must happen before the two become one piece?

c7r20414.text: The manufacturer says that after cooling, the welt and outsole form a single piece of PVC, completing the sole joint.

c7r20416.text: No adhesive is used in this sole-joining operation; the manufacturer describes the connection as heat welded.

c7r20417.text: But once the sole is joined, what must happen to its new edge before the owner can wear the boots again?

c7r20501.text: The repairer first takes the new outsole's edge to another machine and works all around it.

c7r20502.text: Holding the upper, the repairer moves the sole along the rotating tool, changing the boot's angle with each movement of the wrist.

c7r20503.text: What interests me is that the new sole's outer edge is being trimmed, while the signs of wear remain on the upper.

c7r20504.text: What happens to the scuffs on the old upper you wanted to keep?

c7r20505.text: At the workbench, the repairer picks up a cloth and wipes along the shaft and upper, moving their hand around the boot.

c7r20506.text: The cloth passes over the side and the places that have creased. The once-dull upper starts to shine.

c7r20507.text: The repair service lists cleaning, colour restoration and polishing as treatments for upper materials, aiming to restore their appearance as far as possible.

c7r20515.text: What does the repair service need to have ready to remake this joint?

c7r20514.text: The service says it uses original parts wherever possible. Other replacement materials must also be approved by the brand.

c7r20516.text: The annual report says repairing this welted and heat-sealed construction requires specialist machinery and skills.

c7r20517.text: The authorised repair service describes its approach as using the same machines, methods and materials to restore the original construction.

c7r20518.text: The repair service calls the final finishing work hand done. Watch the repairer's hands: where on the boot do they go next?

c7r20519.text: In the demonstration, the hands move to the eyelets, threading the black laces back through one section at a time.

c7r20520.text: The lace goes through a metal eyelet and crosses to the other side. The opening that was spread apart takes on a wearable shape again.

c7r20521.text: With the toe and shaft tidied up, the repairer places a pair of boots back on the bench, with a cardboard box now beside them.

c7r20522.text: How does this pair leave the bench and get back to the person who sent it in?

c7r20601.text: The repairer puts the boots into the box and folds the lid closed. The repair demonstration ends with a parcel ready to post.

c7r20603.text: The July reviewer writes that a few days after receiving the boots, the repair service notified them that the work was done and the boots were on their way back.

c7r20605.text: This customer writes that, one week after Royal Mail collected the parcel, a courier delivered the boots back.

c7r20622.text: When you open the parcel, what will you see besides the repaired boots?

c7r20606.text: The reviewer praises the join and the outsoles.

c7r20607.text: The review also specifically mentions an extra set of brand-new laces.

c7r20608.text: I like that detail: the owner sent away a used pair of boots, and even tying them again now involves something new.

c7r20609.text: They say they were very happy with both the repair and the return time, and would use the service again.

c7r20610.text: Another customer wrote in January 2025: when they put their feet back in, what pleased them most?

c7r20611.text: That review says the new soles, welts and stitching looked great: like having new boots without going through the break-in period again.

c7r20613.text: If you send boots in now, how long does the website estimate you'll wait?

c7r20614.text: The website currently estimates up to about three weeks, and the service only accepts UK customers.

c7r20615.text: After the boots return, the repair service also advises removing dirt first, choosing care products for the upper material, and caring for them regularly.

c7r20619.text: For the July reviewer, the uppers they wanted to keep came home with the repaired boots.

c7r20620.text: What about you: would you keep a creased, worn-in pair and replace the soles, or start wearing a new pair? Tell me in the comments.

c7r20621.text: Subscribe to Brand Stories, and we'll keep looking at how familiar everyday objects are made, used and kept in our lives.
